q: What is the encoder–decoder bottleneck?
short: In RNN seq2seq, the whole source is compressed into one fixed-size vector (the final encoder state); longer inputs must share the same capacity, so information is lost and quality drops with length.

q: Write the RNN recurrence and explain weight sharing.
short: hₜ = tanh(W_h hₜ₋₁ + W_x xₜ + b); the same matrices are used at every step, so the model handles any length with a fixed number of parameters.
detail: Unrolled = deep network with tied weights.

q: Why do gradients vanish in RNNs?
short: Backpropagation through time multiplies one Jacobian per step (W_h times tanh slope); with norms below 1 the product shrinks exponentially, so early inputs get almost no learning signal.

q: How does an LSTM preserve information?
short: Its cell state is updated additively, Cₜ = fₜCₜ₋₁ + iₜC̃ₜ; when the forget gate is near 1, information and gradients flow across many steps; input and output gates control writing and reading.

q: Explain attention in a seq2seq model.
short: At each decoder step, score every encoder state against the decoder state, softmax the scores into weights, and use the weighted sum as the context for generating the next word.
mistakes: Using one context for all steps.

q: Write scaled dot-product attention.
short: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V: queries compare with all keys, scores scaled by √dₖ, softmax per query, then a weighted sum of values.

q: Why do Transformers need positional encodings?
short: Self-attention treats the input as a set; without position information, permuting words permutes outputs identically. Adding sinusoidal or learned position vectors injects order.

q: How is BERT pre-trained?
short: Masked language modelling (15% of tokens selected; 80% [MASK], 10% random, 10% unchanged; predict them using both sides) and next sentence prediction (is B the true continuation of A?).

q: Compute h₁ and h₂ for 'I don't' with W_h = 0.5I, W_x = I, b = 0.
Compute the attention weights and context for s = [1, 0], h₁ = [1, 1], h₂ = [0, 1].
What do multi-head attention and W^O do?
short: Each head projects Q, K, V into a lower-dimensional subspace and attends independently, capturing different relations; outputs are concatenated and mixed by W^O back to model dimension.
detail: Same total cost as one full-size head.

q: Padding mask vs look-ahead mask?
short: Padding mask blocks attention to [PAD] keys used to equalise batch lengths (encoder and decoder); look-ahead mask blocks attention to future positions in the decoder so training matches left-to-right generation.
follow: Does BERT use a look-ahead mask?

q: Why residual connections and LayerNorm?
short: Residuals give gradients a direct path through many layers and let each sub-layer learn a refinement; LayerNorm stabilises activation scales per token, enabling deep, fast training.

q: Static vs contextual embeddings?
short: Static (Word2Vec, GloVe): one vector per word type, conflating senses. Contextual (BERT): a vector per token computed from the whole sentence, distinguishing river bank from money bank.
follow: Can you get a static vector from BERT?

q: Why did Transformers replace RNNs?
short: Parallel computation over positions (fast training on GPUs), constant path length between any two words (long-range dependencies), and better scaling with data and parameters; cost: O(n²) attention.
example: 50 sequential RNN steps vs 1 per layer.

q: Why divide attention scores by √dₖ?
short: For random vectors with unit-variance components, q·k has variance dₖ; large scores push softmax into saturated regions with tiny gradients. Dividing by √dₖ keeps the variance ≈ 1.

q: Explain BERT's 80/10/10 masking strategy.
short: [MASK] never appears at fine-tuning time; replacing some selected tokens with random words or leaving them unchanged forces the model to build good representations for every token, not just masked positions, reducing pre-train/fine-tune mismatch.
detail: Only selected positions contribute to the loss.

q: Fine-tune BERT for extractive question answering.
short: Input [CLS] question [SEP] passage [SEP]; add two vectors scoring each passage token as answer start and end; train with cross-entropy on gold spans; at inference pick the best valid (start ≤ end, length-limited) span; handle long passages with sliding windows.

q: BERT vs GPT-style models?
short: BERT: encoder-only, bidirectional, trained with MLM; best for understanding tasks with fine-tuning. GPT: decoder-only with causal masks, trained to predict the next token; natural for generation and prompting. Encoder–decoder (T5) does both.
mistakes: Using BERT to generate long text.

q: What are the limits of attention-based models on long documents?
short: Self-attention costs O(n²) time and memory, so context windows are limited; remedies include sparse/local attention, linear-attention approximations, memory-efficient kernels, chunking with retrieval (RAG, M14) and recurrence-like state.
